title: Recent Outages Have Economic Causes
summary_raw:
This essay originally appeared in The Guardian. It’s an expanded version of the one I posted as “We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For.”

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyberattack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyberattack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences...

title: We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For
summary_raw:
This essay originally appeared as part of a round table in The Free Press entitled “Is America’s Infrastructure Under Attack?”

Microsoft, the FAA, banks, United Airlines, the NSA—it’s been a really bad week in cyberspace. But, amazing as it might seem, these are not related. As far as we know, they’re not the result of cyberattacks. They’re not even related to AI. (Well, that’s mostly true. The NSA will probably never tell us what went wrong.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

Our computerized infrastructure is vulnerable and fragile. Much of it is old, and has been incrementally patched and upgraded. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. And more and more of it is centralized: the same systems affecting many different aspects of our lives and society. In many cases, it just barely works. And when it fails, it tends to fail badly...

title: Dave Täht given the Jonathan B. Postel Service Award
summary_raw:
The Internet Society has announced that the Jonathan B. Postel Service Award has been awarded to Dave Täht for his many efforts to improve the Internet.

Täht's legacy can be found in community hubs in Nicaragua, where he worked to expand connectivity, and first discovered the urgency of solving bufferbloat. It can be found in every lag-free video call with a loved one. It can be found in outer space—Täht helped Starlink solve its latency challenges. And it can be found in the countless people he mentored and befriended over the years, who will not stop until bufferbloat stops getting in the way of band practice.

Dave is still deeply missed by those of us who knew him; this is an award he richly deserved.

title: [$] Tainting (or not) on manual driver binding
summary_raw: Early in the 7.4 merge window, Greg Kroah-Hartman applied a patch that caused the kernel to be marked as tainted whenever user space manually binds or unbinds a device driver to a device. This change was meant to be a defense against a flood of spurious bug reports generated by fuzzers, but it also turned out to get in the way of some real use cases. After some discussion, the patch has been reverted, but this situation hints at an area where better kernel interfaces are needed.

title: Beyls: Wrapping up LLVM's relicensing effort
summary_raw:
Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. New contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...]

Today, more than 99.5% of all lines of code ever contributed to LLVM are either covered by the new license, too small for copyright to apply, or no longer in the repository.

Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.
